CausalChain: Tumor cells exhibit high glycolytic activity -> Increased lactate secretion into TME -> Uptake of lactate by MDSCs -> Lactate induces histone lactylation in MDSCs -> Upregulation of immunosuppressive genes (e.g., ARG1, iNOS) -> Enhanced T cell suppression and immune evasion -> Tumor progression
Hypothesis: Tumor-derived lactate promotes histone lactylation in MDSCs, epigenetically reprogramming them to a more potent immunosuppressive state; thus, targeting lactate production or blocking lactate-induced histone modifications can impair MDSC function and enhance the efficacy of cancer immunotherapies.
Abstract: Recent evidence indicates that the immunosuppressive capabilities of myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) play a pivotal role in cancer progression and resistance to immunotherapies. Here, we propose that lactate, a key metabolic byproduct of tumor glycolysis, acts as an epigenetic modulator of MDSCs through histone lactylation. Elevated lactate levels in the tumor microenvironment (TME) may be taken up by MDSCs, leading to lactylation of histones that drives the transcription of genes involved in immune suppression, such as ARG1 and iNOS. This metabolic–epigenetic crosstalk could enhance the suppressive functions of MDSCs, thereby facilitating tumor immune escape. Inhibition of lactate production or the blockade of lactate-induced histone modifications may revert the suppressive phenotype of MDSCs, offering a novel therapeutic approach to bolster cancer immunotherapies.
